newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England urges moderate interest rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Bank of England urges moderate interest rate rise.

text.p: The Bank of England said it continued to see the need for a moderate tightening of monetary policy to ensure the government's 2.5 percent inflation target can be met two years ahead.
"The Bank's central projection for inflation two years ahead is close to three percent and rising," it said in its quarterly Inflation Report.

"In the near term, the rise in the exchange rate leads to a fall in the central projection because of lower import prices. But monetary policy must look beyond these short-term effects and ensure that underlying inflation is consistent with the target."
"In the light of the central projection and the risks surrounding it, the Bank continues to see the need for a moderate tightening of policy."

The report did not specify how big a rate increase the Bank would like to see. But deputy governor Howard Davies said on Tuesday the Bank favoured an early quarter-point rise from the present 6.0 percent, perhaps followed by another rise later this year.
The Bank's chief economist Mervyn King told a news conference that the longer the delay in raising interest rates, the greater the increase would have to be to achieve the same effect.
The Bank said that in recent months, there had been little sign of any further acceleration of demand.

"But the case for some tightening in policy does not depend upon a further acceleration. The growth rates of money and demand that have been seen for some time now cannot be sustained for long if the inflation target is to be met two years or so ahead,"it added.
It was now more likely that 12-month RPIX inflation (the underlying rate which excludes mortgage interest payments) would fall below 2.5 percent some time this year.

"The central projection for inflation in two years time is close to that made in November: the adverse effect of lower net external demand is balanced by slightly higher domestic demand and the reversal of some of the earlier falls in import prices," the Bank said.
The uncertainty surrounding the central projection was slightly greater than in November.

"The risks are a little skewed towards the upside. That reflects the risks around the outlook for final domestic demand -- the chances of consumption and investment growing more rapidly than in the central case are higher than the chances of slower growth."

"The uncertainty about the speed of pass-through from the exchange rate to retail prices has increased the risks in the near term in particular, simply because the change in the exchange rate since last summer is larger," the Bank added.
The report said both demand and output were now growing at above-trend rates.
The picture had been complicated by the appreciation of sterling, which would lead to a fall in inflation in the short term as import prices fell.
"But that is primarily a one-off impact on the domestic price level," the Bank said. "The rise in sterling will also lead to a deterioration in net trade performance."
It said the yield curve at the short end had already moved up, anticipating a rise in official interest rates and helping to moderate the expansion of demand.
"If official rates do not rise, the yield curve will fall back, further stimulating the growth of domestic demand," the Bank added.
